## Is your "best" model a real choice, or a fragile artifact of a few periods?

`selectionfragility` gives you two complementary, decision-oriented diagnostics for forecast
**model selection**:

- **Model Confidence Set (MCS)** — which models are statistically *indistinguishable* from the
  best (Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2011). A set of size 1 means the best model is **point-identified**;
  a larger set means selection is **not identified** — the data cannot support crowning one model
  over its rivals.
- **Decision breakdown point (`k*`)** — the *fewest evaluation periods whose deletion flips the
  pooled winner*. A small `k*` means the crowned model rests on a handful of periods (often a
  single shock) and should not be trusted as a stable choice.

This is the native R port of the Python package
[`selection-fragility`](https://pypi.org/project/selection-fragility/) (same method, same
validated numerics, independently verified against it). Function names and signatures are
near-identical 1:1 across the two (`loss_panel()` ≈ `LossPanel.from_losses()`, `report()`,
`decision_breakdown()`, `mcs_size()`, `identified()`, `compare()`, `pooled_winner(L, w)`, ...), and
the VERDICT/LEADERBOARD/RESOLUTION/PIVOT report sections are structured identically in both
languages. Cite either implementation; they compute the same quantities. If you work in Python
instead of R, use `pip install selection-fragility`.

**Two things do NOT carry over if you are switching from the Python package, or running both side
by side during a migration:**

- **`LossPanel.from_forecasts()` has no R equivalent yet.** Python's `from_forecasts(df, y_true=,
  period=, group=)` ingests a wide forecast-vs-actual frame directly (e.g. from
  `statsforecast`/`neuralforecast`'s `cross_validation()`) and computes the per-period loss for
  you. This R port only takes an already-computed loss panel (`loss_panel()`, below) — compute
  your per-period losses yourself first (e.g. `abs(actual - forecast)` per model per period,
  pivoted to one column per model) before calling `loss_panel()`.
- **Bootstrap-based numbers will NOT match the Python package bit-for-bit on "the same" seed.**
  `winner_stability()`, the Model Confidence Set's bootstrap p-value, and `compare()`'s
  permutation churn rate all depend on a random-number stream, and R's RNG and NumPy's RNG are
  different generators — `seed = 0` in both languages draws different resamples. Compare
  *conclusions* (is the champion identified, is `winner_stability` near the exchangeable
  benchmark) across the two implementations, never exact decimals of a bootstrap statistic.

## Installation

```r
# From CRAN, once released:
install.packages("selectionfragility")

# Right now, from GitHub:
# remotes::install_github("sudhanshurai360/selectionfragility")
```

## Quick start

The input is a **loss panel**: a per-period loss (lower is better — e.g. MASE, RMSE, absolute
error) for each candidate model, over the same set of evaluation periods.

```{r setup}
library(selectionfragility)

# Ten years of losses for three models: ar1 is steady, nbeats wins nine of the ten years
# but one shock-year loss (2.60) is large enough that ar1 wins on the pooled mean anyway,
# ets is uniformly worse.
L <- list(
  ar1    = c(1.00, 0.98, 1.02, 1.01, 0.99, 1.03, 0.97, 1.00, 1.02, 0.98),
  nbeats = c(0.90, 0.88, 0.92, 0.91, 0.89, 0.93, 0.87, 0.90, 2.60, 0.88),
  ets    = c(1.20, 1.18, 1.22, 1.21, 1.19, 1.23, 1.17, 1.20, 1.22, 1.18)
)

panel <- loss_panel(L)
report(panel)   # auto-prints; print(report(panel)) and cat(report(panel)) both also work
```

This one-screen report has four sections:

- **VERDICT** — is the best model point-identified (the Model Confidence Set)?
- **LEADERBOARD** — mean loss, MCS membership, and how many periods each model actually won.
- **RESOLUTION** — is the observed edge over the closest rival statistically significant at this
  sample size, versus what sample size *would* resolve it (minimum detectable edge)?
- **PIVOT** — `k*`, which specific periods are responsible, and how concentrated the champion's
  win is in a single period.

Read this example's own output carefully, because it is deliberately **not** a clean case, and
that is the point. `ar1` is the pooled champion, but VERDICT says **not identified** (the Model
Confidence Set has two members — `ar1` and `nbeats` are statistically tied), and PIVOT reports
`k*=1`: deleting just the single responsible period would flip the pooled winner to `nbeats`.
Because the champion is not identified, PIVOT's fragility read is explicitly **UNDETERMINED** — the
package tells you the `k*=1` fact (that part is always shown, since it is a deterministic property
of the data), but refuses to also certify it as "non-significant" or interpret `concentration_share`
on top of an undetermined decision. **This refusal is the central design discipline of the whole
package (its "R1/R2 rules" — see `?resolution_report`): never print a confident-looking
interpretive number on a decision the data cannot actually support.** The headline "ar1 wins" is
real on the full sample, but — as VERDICT, RESOLUTION, and PIVOT's own UNDETERMINED flag all
agree — it is not a robust, well-separated decision.

### Name your periods

Without `labels=`, periods are reported by **position, 0-indexed** (`k*=1 of 10 periods (8)` for
the 9th period) — matching the Python package's own default positional labels, not R's usual
1-based counting. This is deliberate for cross-language consistency, but it means the bare number
in an unlabeled report is one less than the period's 1-based position if you count by hand. Pass
real labels and avoid the ambiguity entirely:

```{r}
years <- 2015:2024
panel2 <- loss_panel(L, labels = years)
report(panel2)
```

PIVOT now names the responsible year directly (`2023`) instead of a bare index.

### Watch out: loss direction is not checked

This package assumes **lower is better** throughout — it is built on loss panels (MASE, RMSE,
absolute error, and similar). If you feed it *accuracy*-style data instead (anything where
*higher* is better, e.g. classification accuracy or R²), nothing raises an error: you get a fully
confident, silently **inverted** answer, because the worst model by your own metric gets crowned
the winner. There is no way for the package to know your metric's direction, so it is entirely on
you to pass loss, not accuracy.

## Core functions, one stage at a time

`report()` is the recommended entry point, but every statistic behind it is also a public
function, in case you want just one number or to check a published result against the code
directly.

**Calling convention:** every function below accepts EITHER a plain named list `L` (as built
above) OR a `loss_panel` object — except that **only a `loss_panel` carries labels and weights**.
If you built `panel <- loss_panel(L, labels = years)`, call these on `panel`, not on the bare `L`
— passing `labels = years` directly to a Stage 1+ function (e.g. `decision_breakdown(L, labels =
years)`) is not supported and raises an "unused argument" error. `report()` is the one function
that *requires* a `loss_panel` (it reads `panel$weights`/`panel$labels` directly) and is the only
one that resolves `k*`'s responsible periods into real labels for display — see the note on
`decision_breakdown()`'s `removed` field below.

```{r}
# Stage 0 — the validated panel itself (carries labels and weights; build it once, reuse it)
panel <- loss_panel(L, labels = years)

# Stage 1 — is the best model identified?
mcs_size(panel)        # size of the Model Confidence Set; 1 = point-identified
identified(panel)       # TRUE iff mcs_size(panel) == 1

# Stage 2 — is the observed edge resolved at this sample size?
resolution_report(panel)

# Stage 3 — the decision breakdown point itself
decision_breakdown(panel)
```

`decision_breakdown()$removed` above is a bare, 1-based **position** into the loss vectors, not a
resolved label — even though `panel` was built with `labels = years`. Only `report()` resolves
`k*`'s responsible periods into actual labels for display; if you need them from
`decision_breakdown()` directly, index into the panel yourself: `panel$labels[decision_breakdown(panel)$removed]`.

```{r}
# Stage 4 — how concentrated is the champion's win in a single period?
concentration_share(panel)
```

`pooled_winner()`, `per_period_winner()`, `condorcet_winner()`/`condorcet_status()`, and
`fragility()` sit underneath these and are documented on their own help pages (`?fragility`) —
reach for them when you want every diagnostic field in one call, or need the lower-level numbers a
paper's results table was computed from. `surprise_concentration()` answers a related but distinct
question — not "is the champion's win fragile" but "is the panel's own task difficulty
concentrated in one period" — see `?surprise_concentration`.

## Weights

Pass `w=` to weight periods unequally (for example, by observation count):

```{r}
w <- c(4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 1, 4)  # the shock year carries less weight
pooled_winner(L, w)
```

Most functions accept `w=` directly; a `loss_panel` built with weights carries them automatically,
so `report(panel)` picks them up without repeating them.

## Gating a CI/pipeline promotion step

If you re-run a model comparison on a schedule (e.g. a weekly retrain), `compare()` answers "the
champion changed this week — is that signal or noise?":

```{r}
previous <- loss_panel(L, labels = years)

# A new evaluation period (2025) arrives, and in it nbeats has a big edge -- add one new value
# to EVERY model's vector, not just one, since all models in a panel must share the same periods.
L_new_period <- list(ar1 = c(L$ar1, 1.00), nbeats = c(L$nbeats, 0.50), ets = c(L$ets, 1.20))
current <- loss_panel(L_new_period, labels = c(years, 2025))

compare(previous, current)
```

`compare(previous, current)` reports whether the pooled champion changed, whether that change is
attributable to the newly-arrived period(s) specifically, whether the old champion has genuinely
left the Model Confidence Set, and a permutation-based estimate of how often a champion "changes"
out of pure noise alone at this panel's size. Its `$act` field is the single boolean a promotion
step should gate on.

## Honest reporting — what this package will not do for you

- **`mcs_size(L) > 1` can reflect low statistical power, not just a genuine tie** — especially at
  small `T`. Read it as *"cannot be distinguished at this sample size,"* never as *"these models
  are equivalent."*
- **`winner_stability()` is not interpretable on its own.** Compare it to
  `exchangeable_benchmark(K, T)` — the distribution this same statistic takes when no model is
  truly better. Values in the 0.4–0.6 range are often exactly what chance alone produces:

  ```{r}
  ws <- winner_stability(L)
  ws$stability

  bench <- exchangeable_benchmark(K = 3, T = 10, n_rep = 50, n_boot = 200)  # small n_rep/n_boot for a fast vignette build
  bench   # median, p05, p95 of winner_stability under "no model is truly better"
  ```

  A `winner_stability` value is only unusually fragile *relative to chance* if it falls below
  `bench$p05` for your own panel's actual `K` (model count) and `T` (period count).
- **`k*` is a descriptive fact about the observed data, not a hypothesis test** — no
  multiple-comparisons correction applies to it. `mcb_bound()` *is* a corrected confidence bound
  for the same post-hoc rival-selection problem:

  ```{r}
  mcb_bound(L)   # "the champion's true edge over its binding rival may be as large as X%, at 95% confidence"
  ```
- This package was built for a trusted analyst diagnosing their own model comparison, not for an
  adversarial setting where the models being evaluated were chosen knowing the methodology. See
  `?mcs` (its "Adversarial use / competition settings" section) for the gaming vectors to guard
  against before using an MCS "tie" claim in a competition or leaderboard context.

See the companion paper for the full power/false-discovery tables and derivations behind these
statistics.
